newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief still opts for troops in Eastern Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief still opts for troops in Eastern Zaire.

text.p: The United Nations said on Monday that a military force was still needed in eastern Zaire despite allied plans to scale down or eliminate plans for troops and use air drops of food instead.

In a report to the Security Council, Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said "a practical way to avoid a humanitarian disaster is the establishment of some form of military presence in the region."

In the last three week, plans for an international force to help refugees, particularly those from Rwanda, have been reduced from a proposed 15,000-member military force in eastern Zaire to a logistical team based in Uganda to see if relief can be air-dropped.

But Boutros-Ghali said that hundreds of thousands of men, women and children were still facing hunger, disease and violent death, most of them scattered in inaccessible and inhospitable areas of eastern Zaire.
He said that as of Nov. 25, up to 700,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees and displaced Zairians were believed to be in the area.
The refugees, he said, should be the first priority. He warned that "there must be no return to the status quo ante and above all no re-creation of the refugee camps in eastern Zaire."

Rwanda and its allies dispute the U.N. statistics, estimating the number of refugees as less than 200,000. Many of the remaining refugees are also thought to be travelling with Rwandan Hutu soldiers and militias who controlled the camps and had a role in the 1994 genocide of Rwandan Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

The Hutu soldiers are being attacked by Zairian rebels of Tutsi origin who have ties to the current Tutsi-led Rwandan government. Some aid workers fear that food dropped from the air would fall into the hands of armed groups, who would control distribution of the goods.
